analysis.one_liner: Repeals Obamacare rules forcing insurers to spend premiums on care and rebate the rest.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill; it sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee and its health subcommittee from June 2011 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the Affordable Care Act's medical loss ratio rule, which requires health insurers to spend a set share of premiums — 80-85% depending on the market — on actual medical care and quality improvement, and to mail rebate checks to customers when they fall short [S2][S3]. It would also repeal a rule requiring every hospital to publish its standard charges for items and services [S2][S3]. The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in the House [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers would keep premium dollars they are currently required to return to customers through rebates when they spend too little on care. Hospitals would no longer have to publish their standard charge lists, shielding their pricing from public comparison [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the requirement that insurers spend at least 80% of premiums in individual and small-group markets and 85% in large-group markets on clinical services and quality improvement, and rebate the difference to enrollees if they miss the mark [S2][S3].
It repeals the requirement that each U.S. hospital establish and make public a list of its standard charges, ending the only federal rule then requiring hospitals to disclose prices [S2][S3].
It applies to all plans, including grandfathered plans that were otherwise exempt from most ACA insurance rules [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Insurance customers would lose the annual rebate checks the rule produces when insurers keep too much of their premiums, and patients would lose access to hospital standard-charge lists that let them compare prices [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Repealing the medical loss ratio would end the rebate mechanism that returned premium dollars to enrollees when insurers spent too little on care, shifting that money back to insurer margins [S2][S3].

Repealing hospital charge transparency would remove the public's ability to see what hospitals say their services cost, which supporters of the original requirement saw as a first step toward price competition [S2].

Insurers argued the ratio rules forced excessive paperwork and could push firms out of some markets; the bill's supporters raised these compliance burdens, though the bill text addresses them only by full repeal [S1][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow to insurers and hospitals, not to the public: its only substantive provisions remove consumer protections and disclosure requirements. Insurers' compliance-cost arguments were not addressed by restructuring the rule — the bill simply repealed the protections entirely.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Price introduced the bill on June 1, 2011, with Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers as the other original sponsor, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S3][S5].
Two days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, the last action it ever received [S5].
Despite 81 cosponsors — 80 Republicans and 1 Democrat — the committee never scheduled a markup and the House never voted on it before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insured consumers are better off because the bill died: they kept the legal right to MLR rebates and hospital charge disclosure. Insurers and hospitals did not get the repeal they sought, and the status quo of the ACA's insurance rules stayed in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insured consumers, who kept rebate rights

for.name: Rep. Tom Price
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the ACA's medical loss ratio and hospital price transparency requirements [S1][S3][S5].

for.name: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced [S3].

for.name: 80 House Republicans and 1 House Democrat
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it broad House Republican support on paper [S4].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: The committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or any further committee action on the bill after referring it to the health subcommittee, so it never reached the floor [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Republican — 80 of the 81 cosponsors were House Republicans, with a single Democratic cosponsor — and the bill never advanced past a subcommittee referral [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would let insurers keep premium dollars they currently must spend on care or refund to customers, directly ending the MLR rebate mechanism. Its gain comes out of policyholders' pockets [S2][S3].

The bill repeals the federal requirement that every hospital publish a list of standard charges, letting hospitals keep their prices from public comparison. Patients lose the ability to see posted prices [S2][S3].
